
  Caching happens at several layers. First, the operating system on the
  client machine typically maintains a local stub cache (via
  systemd-resolved, dnsmasq, the Windows DNS Client service, or
  browser-internal caches in some cases). Second, recursive resolvers —
  run by ISPs or public providers like Google (8.8.8.8) or Cloudflare
  (1.1.1.1) — hold the largest and most important caches, shared across
  many users. Browser and application-level caches (like Java's or
  Chrome's DNS caches) add another layer above that.

  Each cached record carries a TTL (time to live), set by the
  authoritative zone. The resolver decrements TTLs as time passes, and
  once a record's TTL expires it must be re-fetched from the
  authoritative source. TTLs trade freshness against load: short TTLs
  (30–300s) propagate changes quickly but increase query volume; long
  TTLs (hours to days) reduce traffic but mean stale records linger
  after changes like server migrations.

  A subtle but important detail is negative caching: RFC 2308 says
  resolvers should also cache NXDOMAIN and NODATA responses so that
  lookups for nonexistent names don't hammer authoritative servers.

  Caching can cause real-world headaches: DNS-based failover is slowed
  by stale caches, CDN steering can serve a user a far-off node, and
  misconfigured resolvers that ignore TTLs cause broken deployments.
  Operators mitigate this by lowering TTLs before planned changes,
  flushing caches explicitly (ipconfig /flushdns, resolvectl
  flush-caches), and relying on resolver operators to honor TTLs
  correctly.

  DONE

  on how TCP congestion control evolved. End with DONE.
